parsed.note: The popular absolute claim '50 percent of marriages in the United States end in divorce' is a flattened, unsourced paraphrase of a conditional demographic projection first formally published by Paul Glick (1984), who stated 'about one-half of the first marriages of young adults today are likely to end in divorce' — a cohort projection for people marrying circa 1980 that was subsequently cited without its conditionality, misapplied to all marriages at all times, and further confused with a flawed crude-rate calculation (annual divorces ÷ annual marriages ≈ 50%).

chain.title: Divorce Statistics and Facts | What Affects Divorce Rates in the U.S.?
chain.exact_wording: Almost 50 percent of all marriages in the United States will end in divorce or separation.
chain.change: Claim presented as a standing fact for all marriages with no citation to any source; 'almost 50%' conflates divorce and separation and strips all conditionality from the original projection.

chain.title: Can this marriage be saved? – APA Monitor on Psychology
chain.exact_wording: experts routinely estimate that between 40 percent and 50 percent of marriages today will end in divorce.
chain.change: APA hedges with 'experts routinely estimate' and a range (40–50%), attributing underlying data to NCHS rather than to any single primary projection study; does not name Glick, Preston, or any originating paper.

chain.title: Marriage, Divorce, and Remarriage in the 1990's – U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Reports P23-180
chain.exact_wording: Between the late 1960's and 1980, the divorce rate doubled, reaching a level where at least 1 out of 2 marriages was expected to end in divorce (Castro Martin and Bumpass, 1989).
chain.change: Census report itself cites Castro Martin and Bumpass (1989) for the '1 out of 2' figure, and separately projects 4-out-of-10 or 5-out-of-10 depending on trend assumption — the report does not originate the claim but transmits it; also cites Norton and Moorman (1987) as an earlier survey source.

chain.title: What Is the Divorce Rate, Anyway? Around 42 Percent, One Scholar Believes – Institute for Family Studies
chain.exact_wording: in 1984, Paul Glick published a study saying, among other things, 'About one-half of the first marriages of young adults today are likely to end in divorce.'
chain.change: Article correctly identifies Glick (1984) as the earliest named formal source of the projection and notes the origin is hard to trace further back; also attributes crude-rate misuse as a parallel popularising mechanism.

chain.title: Breaking Up Is Hard to Count: The Rise of Divorce in the United States, 1980–2010 – Demography (PMC)
chain.exact_wording: By the 1980s, most demographic analysts agreed that about one-half of marriages then being contracted would end in divorce (e.g., Cherlin 1981; Glick 1984; Norton 1983).
chain.change: Peer-reviewed article confirms that by the 1980s the consensus projection was ~50%, attributing it to Cherlin (1981), Glick (1984), and Norton (1983); also notes Preston (1975) estimated 44% using indirect methods from 1973 disruption rates — pushing the traceable chain back to Preston (1975).

chain.title: Determinants of Divorce over the Marital Life Course – American Sociological Review, Vol. 51 No. 4 (South & Spitze 1986)
chain.exact_wording: recent projections suggest that close to half of recent marriages will end in divorce (Preston and McDonald, 1979; Cherlin, 1981).
chain.change: 1986 peer-reviewed paper cites Preston and McDonald (1979) and Cherlin (1981) as the sources of the 'close to half' projection — pushing the earliest traceable named primary source back to Preston & McDonald (1979), predating Glick (1984).

chain.title: Breaking Up Is Hard to Count – Demography (PMC) [second reference for Preston 1975]
chain.exact_wording: Preston (1975) used indirect methods to estimate that 44% of marriages would end in divorce based on the disruption rates observed in 1973.
chain.change: Identifies Preston (1975) as producing a quantitative estimate of 44% — the earliest named primary calculation in the evidence chain — based on 1973 NCHS disruption-rate data, predating Preston & McDonald (1979).

chain.title: Vital and Health Statistics Series 21, No. 24 – NCHS (December 1973)
chain.exact_wording: In 1967 there were more than 50 times as many divorces in the United States as in 1867 (10,000 to 523,000) but only 5.4 times as many marriages (357,000 to 1,927,000).
chain.change: This NCHS vital-statistics compendium (1867–1967 data) is the underlying federal dataset from which Preston (1975) drew 1973 disruption rates to construct his 44% estimate; it does not itself state a 50% lifetime figure but provides the raw annual marriage and divorce counts that made the crude-rate calculation possible.

searched_but_not_found: APA.org primary topic page on divorce (apa.org/topics/divorce-child-custody) — states no 50% figure and cites no originating study
CDC NCHS FastStats Marriage and Divorce (cdc.gov/nchs/fastats/marriage-divorce.htm) — reports current annual rates only; no 50% lifetime claim or originating source

CDC/NCHS Advance Data No. 323, Bramlett & Mosher 2001 (stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/108336) — reports 1/5 of first marriages end within 5 years and 1/3 within 10 years; does not state a 50% lifetime figure
CDC/NCHS Vital and Health Statistics Series 23 No. 22, July 2002 (cdc.gov/nchs/data/series/sr_23/sr23_022.pdf) — life-table probabilities by characteristic; no 50% lifetime figure in front matter
Preston & McDonald (1979) original journal article — named in chain but full text not directly retrieved; existence confirmed by South & Spitze (1986) citation
Paul Glick (1984) original study — named in chain but full text not directly retrieved; existence and exact wording confirmed by IFS blog citation
Preston (1975) original paper — named in chain but full text not retrieved; existence confirmed by Kennedy/Ruggles (2014) PMC article
